title: Vice-President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan Expresses Grief over the Demise of Music Composer Deva
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 3:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Vice-President of India, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan, has expressed deep sorrow over the demise of renowned music composer Deva.
In his condolence message, the Vice-President said that Deva had carved a distinct identity for himself in the Tamil film industry through his unique musical style and popular ‘gaana’ songs that captured the lives and emotions of people. He noted that Deva had composed music for over 400 films in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada, making a lasting contribution to Indian cinema.
The Vice-President said that Deva’s memorable compositions and distinctive contribution to 'gaana' music would continue to be cherished by generations of music lovers. He described the composer’s demise as a great loss to the Tamil film and music industry.
Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan extended his heartfelt condolences to the bereaved family, relatives, friends, members of the film fraternity and music lovers.

title: AIIA Marks Its 10th Foundation Day with Two MoUs, Major Academic Publications and Digital Launches
subtitle: KAUMARACON 2026 Concludes with Global Deliberations on Ayurvedic Child Healthcare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 9:38PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The three-day International Conference on Kaumarabhritya,
KAUMARACON 2026
, organised by the All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi, through its Department of Kaumarabhritya, concluded on Saturday with international scientific deliberations on advancing Ayurvedic child healthcare. The concluding day coincided with the Institute’s
10th Foundation Day
, celebrating a decade of progress in Ayurveda education, research, clinical excellence and global collaboration.
The conference brought together international experts, academicians, researchers, clinicians, policymakers and industry representatives to discuss the role of Ayurveda and Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCIM) in paediatric healthcare, emphasising scientific validation, interdisciplinary research and preventive care.
The scientific session on
Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine (TCIM) in Global Child Health
featured perspectives from experts representing the United Kingdom, Sri Lanka, Germany, Nepal, Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Italy and the United States, among other countries. Discussions covered Ayurvedic paediatric education, regulatory frameworks, traditional medicine practices and opportunities for international collaboration in child healthcare. A panel discussion on
Industry–Academia Synergies: Catalyzing Research, Innovation, and Commercialization in Child Healthcare
, chaired by
Prof. (Vd.) P. K. Prajapati, Director, AIIA
, with
Dr. A. Raghu, Advisor (Ayurveda), Ministry of Ayush
, as co-chair, explored research-driven product development, quality assurance and the translation of academic findings into accessible healthcare solutions. A round-table conference on
Policy, Education, and Research in Kaumarabhritya
further examined strategies to strengthen Ayurvedic paediatrics through specialised education, research and policy support.
The Foundation Day ceremony was graced by
Shri Ramvir Singh Bidhuri, Hon’ble Member of Parliament, Lok Sabha
, as Chief Guest;
Padma Bhushan Vaidya Devendra Triguna Ji
and
Prof. Dr. Abhimanyu Kumar,
Former Director, AIIA and CEO, CAYEIT
,
as Guests of Honour; and
Dr. Ashok Kumar Varshney, National Organising Secretary, Arogya Bharati and Member, National Medical Commission
, as Special Guest.
Prof. (Vd.) P. K. Prajapati, Director, AIIA
, was also present. A major highlight was the signing of two Memorandum of Understanding between AIIA and
Rashtriya Ayurved Vidyapeeth
, and AIIA and
Arogya Bharati
, to strengthen institutional collaboration and knowledge-sharing in Ayurveda
.
More than 15 academic publications and educational resources were launched. The Institute also launched its new
Digital Brand Identity Manual (DBIM)-compliant website
, the e-course
Foundations of Entrepreneurship & Startup Development for Ayush Professionals (FESDAP)
, and
A Textbook of Research Methodology and Medical Statistics
. The online launch of the eBook
Rooted and Rising: Journey of All India Institute of Ayurveda
documented the Institute’s institutional journey and achievements.
Congratulating the AIIA family,
Shri Ramvir Singh Bidhuri
,
Hon’ble Member of Parliament, Lok Sabha, said
, “I witnessed the foundation-laying ceremony of AIIA and have seen its remarkable growth from 2016 to 2026. The hospital is doing commendable work, with the Hon’ble Prime Minister extending support at every stage of its growth.”
Thanking the Hon’ble Minister and acknowledging the efforts of the Institute’s team,
Prof. (Vd.) P. K. Prajapati, Director, AIIA
, said, “The success of KAUMARACON 2026 is a result of the tireless efforts of the AIIA family, who have worked day and night to make this conference a grand success.”

title: AIIA recognised as a Centre of Excellence for RAV in Kaumarbhritya
subtitle:
MoU signed at KAUMARACON 2026 to standardise Swarnaprashan and strengthen research and training

International MoU with Maharishi International University provides for an Ayurveda Academic Chair in the USA
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 9:07PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Rashtriya Ayurveda Vidyapeeth (RAV), Ministry of Ayush, during KAUMARACON 2026 at AIIA, New Delhi. The agreement recognises the Department of Kaumarbhritya at AIIA Delhi and Goa as a Centre of Excellence for RAV.
The recognition covers the development of standard operating procedures (SOPs) and training in Kaumarbhritya (Ayurveda paediatrics), along with intellectual property rights and capacity building in policy research. The partnership also envisages research and training in Swarnaprashan and allied areas of Balroga.
A central objective of the MoU is to develop an SOP for Swarnaprashan Samskar through joint expert consultations at AIIA Goa and New Delhi. This work will address formulation standardisation, preparation, administration and dosage appropriate to the age and strength of the child, with attention to quality control, safety, documentation, monitoring and awareness among parents and caregivers.
The collaboration provides for laboratory and clinical research on the safety and efficacy of Swarnaprashan, subject to feasibility and necessary approvals, as well as joint publications and capacity-building programmes. RAV will support technical deliberations and dissemination of the SOP among relevant national and international stakeholders.
AIIA Goa has established PRAYAS, an integrated paediatric neurorehabilitation centre offering a distinctive multidisciplinary model of care. The centre combines a specialised paediatric Panchakarma unit with the expertise of Ayurveda paediatricians, a modern paediatrician, an occupational therapist, a speech therapist, a physiotherapist, Yoga professionals and an Ayurveda diet expert from Swasthavritta which will work with RAV for further training andf capacity building.
These professionals work together to support children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), cerebral palsy (CP), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and other neurodevelopmental conditions. The model aims to improve daily functioning, participation and quality of life through coordinated care tailored to the needs of each child.
An international MoU was also signed between AIIA Goa and Maharishi International University (MIU), Fairfield, Iowa, USA, for the establishment of an Academic Chair in Ayurveda in MIU's Department of Physiology and Health. The agreement provides for academic and research activities, curriculum development, short- and medium-term courses, and workshops, seminars and conferences on Ayurveda.
The Chair will also explore collaborative research and dissemination of research findings, while promoting the safe use of Ayurveda in the United States. The MoU includes provisions for protection of intellectual property generated through the collaboration.

title: World Menopause Day 2026: Ayurveda Promotes Holistic Approach to Menopausal Health
subtitle: Ministry of Ayush Emphasizes Awareness, Preventive Care and Research for Women’s Health During Menopause
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 6:07PM by PIB Delhi
content:
On the occasion of World Menopause Day 2026, observed on 18 October, the Ministry of Ayush is highlighting the importance of awareness, preventive care and comprehensive approaches to women’s health during menopause. Through the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS), the Ministry seeks to promote a better understanding of menopausal health, with attention to physical health, emotional well-being, and quality of life.
Menopause is a natural biological stage, defined as the permanent cessation of menstruation following the loss of ovarian follicular activity. It usually occurs between 45 and 55 years of age. The transition to menopause may be accompanied by a range of physical and psychological changes, including irregular menstruation, hot flushes, vaginal dryness, sleep disturbances, mood changes, joint pain and anxiety. In Ayurveda, symptoms associated with this phase are discussed in the context of Rajonivritti and its associated clinical features. Their recognition and appropriate management are important for supporting women’s health and well-being during this stage of life.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the menopausal transition can be gradual, usually beginning with changes in the menstrual cycle. Perimenopause refers to the period from when these signs are first observed until one year after the final menstrual period. It can last several years and affect physical, emotional, mental and social well-being. Both hormonal and non-hormonal interventions can help alleviate perimenopausal symptoms.
Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary, Ministry of Ayush, Emphasised, “Women’s health requires sustained attention across every stage of life, including the transition through menopause. Ayurveda offers a comprehensive framework that emphasizes prevention, appropriate lifestyle practices and individualized care. The Ministry of Ayush remains committed to strengthening research and scientific validation in this area, while promoting greater awareness of women’s health and approaches that support their well-being and quality of life.”
Prof. Rabinarayan Acharya, Director General, CCRAS, emphasized, “Ayurveda views menopause as a natural transformation, not a disorder. Through the use of Rasayana therapies, dietary guidance, and mental well-being practices, women can transition through this phase with balance and grace. At CCRAS, our research focuses on validating classical formulations such as Ashokarista and Amalaki Rasayana for their effectiveness in supporting hormonal balance, bone health, and emotional resilience. Empowering women through awareness and preventive care remains central to our mission.”
Dr N. Srikanth, Deputy Director General, CCRAS, noted, “Menopause is a natural transition that deserves mindful care. Ayurveda empowers women to navigate this phase with balance, vitality, and confidence through time-tested approaches in diet, Rasayana therapy, yoga, and emotional well-being. Our focus at CCRAS is to translate classical knowledge into evidence-based solutions that enhance women’s holistic health and quality of life.”
Ayurveda provides a multidimensional approach to managing menopausal symptoms through Rasayana (rejuvenation) therapies, dietary guidance, counseling, yoga, and herbal formulations. Key approaches include:
Rasayana and Lifestyle Interventions:
Rejuvenating herbs and appropriate lifestyle modifications are traditionally used to support vitality and address degenerative changes.
Counseling and Emotional Support:
Ayurveda emphasizes mental well-being through self-care, stress management and family support.
Herbal Formulations:
Classical Ayurveda preparations such as Ashokarista, Lodhrasava, Usheerasava, Chandanadi Loha, Amalaki Rasayana and Mukta Shukti are traditionally used in Ayurvedic practice for concerns associated with menopausal health. Their use should be guided by a qualified healthcare professional.
Dietary Guidance:
A balanced, varied diet suited to individual needs can support general health during and after menopause. Ayurvedic dietary recommendations may be individualized according to the person’s constitution, digestive status, and clinical condition. Adequate protein, calcium, and other essential nutrients are particularly important for maintaining muscle strength and bone health.
Yoga and Meditation:
Regular practice of Asanas, Pranayama, meditation, and Dhyaan may support emotional equilibrium, sleep quality and musculoskeletal health. Yoga practices such as Setu Bandhasana, Vipreetkarani Asana, Marjariasana and Shavasana promote relaxation and may help ease stiffness, back pain and fatigue. Breathing techniques such as Sitali Pranayama and Bhramari Pranayama, along with Yoga Nidra, may support relaxation, emotional balance and sleep.
Ayurveda emphasizes balanced dietary and lifestyle habits, including moderation in food intake, avoiding excessive consumption of pungent and salty foods, limiting alcohol, avoiding tobacco, and managing physical and emotional stress.
The Ministry of Ayush and CCRAS continues to advance research on Ayurvedic approaches to women’s health, with a focus on generating scientific evidence, evaluating clinical outcomes, and promoting informed awareness of menopausal health and well-being.
On World Menopause Day 2026, the Ministry of Ayush calls for greater awareness, open conversations and timely, appropriate care to help women navigate menopause with confidence and maintain their health and well-being.

: India’s Space economy, currently valued at around USD 9 billion, is expected to reach USD 40–45 billion over the next seven to eight years, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances, Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, said during a media Roundtable here on “Space, Sovereignty and New Economy”.
The Minister said India must now move beyond demonstrating its technological capabilities to building globally competitive commercial space companies. He stressed that greater domestic and international investment, predictable demand, faster regulatory approvals and sustainable business models would be essential to scaling up Indian enterprises and expanding their presence in global markets.
The Minister participated in the Roundtable organised by the 'Bloomberg New Economy Forum', being held in New Delhi. The discussion examined how countries can translate sovereign Space capabilities into commercially competitive industries, attract private capital and develop stronger supply chains while safeguarding national interests. Participants also discussed the evolving global space economy, the role of international partnerships and the challenges of scaling up private space enterprises.
Among the other prominent participants were  Vinod Kumar, Director (Promotion), Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe); and Aisha Bowe, Founder and CEO of STEMBoard and LINGO, former NASA engineer and Blue Origin astronaut. The session brought together representatives from the Space industry, entrepreneurship, academia and the international space community.
The Minister said the opening of India’s Space sector to private participation in 2019–2020 under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi had produced significant results within just five to six years. India’s experience demonstrates the potential of bringing government institutions and private industry together in a sector that requires substantial technological expertise, investment and long-term commitment. The priority now, he said, is to convert these capabilities into commercially viable businesses with the scale to compete internationally.
Dr. Jitendra Singh stressed that generating demand is essential for the growth of private space companies. Referring to the Government’s use-case-based approach, he said anchor government customers and support for proof-of-concept projects can help enterprises demonstrate their technologies and move towards commercial deployment. A predictable customer base can give companies the confidence to invest in production, develop market-ready products and build sustainable revenue streams.
He also stressed the need for timely regulatory approvals, lower business costs and stronger supply-chain integration. Companies seeking installation or export licences should be able to obtain the necessary approvals within defined timeframes. Referring to GST-related measures for space products, the Minister said reforms must translate into practical benefits for industry. Investment becomes sustainable when businesses have predictable demand, efficient processes and a clear path to commercial growth.
On investment and international cooperation, the Minister said India is opening up opportunities for capital and partnerships while continuing to strengthen indigenous capabilities. Greater investment can support technology development, manufacturing and access to international markets, while domestic capabilities remain important for national security and strategic autonomy.
He called for stronger collaboration between Indian government institutions and private enterprises, complemented by partnerships with international counterparts. This approach can help Indian companies integrate into global supply chains, expand their customer base and contribute to the wider space economy without compromising national interests. The objective is to combine the strengths of public and private enterprises in India with the capabilities of partners abroad.
The Minister said India’s Space programme is distinguished not only by its achievements in space but also by the extensive use of space technology on Earth. Satellite communications, geospatial applications and Earth observation are supporting infrastructure development, project monitoring, agriculture, disaster management and defence.
Dr Jitendra Singh referred to the use of Space technology for project clearances, monitoring implementation timelines and geotagging development works. India is also providing space-based information and support for disaster management to neighbouring countries, including Myanmar, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. These applications demonstrate how investments in space capabilities can improve public services, support development and create opportunities for commercial applications.
The wider economic value of the Space sector, the Minister said, lies in connecting technological achievements with practical applications and the needs of citizens. Alongside launch vehicles and satellites, downstream services, data-driven solutions and industrial applications will be important in expanding the market for Indian space companies.
Dr. Jitendra Singh emphasised that national space capabilities and international cooperation need not be competing objectives. India must continue to build its own technological strengths while working with global partners to expand opportunities for its industry. Stronger domestic and international public-private partnerships can support investment, technology development, supply-chain integration and access to new markets.
The Minister also stressed the importance of remaining open to progressive ideas and adapting policies as technology and industry requirements evolve. The opening of the space sector to private participation reflects the value of enabling new players to contribute alongside established public institutions.
India’s next phase of space-sector growth will depend on turning technological strengths into commercially successful enterprises. Greater investment, predictable demand, efficient regulatory processes, indigenous capabilities and international partnerships will be central to this transition, positioning the country for a larger role in the global space economy.

title: Department of Commerce Organises “Leveraging FTAs” Outreach Programme in Jaipur to Strengthen Export Opportunities

date:

                17 OCT 2026 6:27PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Commerce organised an outreach programme “Leveraging FTAs – Outreach Programme” in Jaipur, Rajasthan, to create awareness about the benefits available under India’s Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and facilitate their effective utilisation by exporters. The programme was addressed by Joint Secretary, Department of Commerce, Shri Mohit Yadav, and witnessed participation from exporters across sectors and representatives of the Government of Rajasthan, Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), Jaipur Special Economic Zone and the Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC).
The programme aimed to help Indian enterprises translate preferential market access under FTAs into export opportunities through targeted information, capacity building, practical guidance and coordination among the Department of Commerce, State Governments, industry associations and exporters.
The programme assumed significance in the context of India’s expanding engagement with the global economy. At the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, the Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi stated, “Our constant endeavour is to ensure that India’s capabilities open new doors of opportunity for other countries as well.” In his Independence Day address on 15 August 2026 and on other occasions, the Prime Minister has highlighted the opportunities created by FTAs for Indian producers, farmers and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), while emphasising the importance of meeting international quality standards to access global markets.
Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal has emphasised the commercial opportunities from India’s FTAs. The Minister has noted that India’s agreements provide preferential access to markets accounting for a major share of global trade This will create numerous jobs and huge opportunities for farmers, women entrepreneurs, youth, MSMEs, artisans and industry. He urged them to make use of reduced- or zero-duty access by focusing on quality. He has highlighted the new market opportunities for Indian industry and businesses opened through India’s recently concluded FTAs. The objective of the outreach programme is to move beyond negotiating market access to helping enterprises actually use it, with targeted information, capacity building, practical guidance and coordination among the Department of Commerce, the State Government, industry associations and exporters.
India’s exports of merchandise and services have continued to register growth. Cumulative exports during April–September 2026–27 are estimated at US$ 476.20 billion, compared with US$ 418.31 billion during the corresponding period of 2025–26, registering estimated growth of 13.84%. Major drivers of merchandise export growth in September 2026 included electronic goods, petroleum products, organic and inorganic chemicals, engineering goods, and cotton yarn, fabrics, made-ups and handloom products.
The programme provided a platform for exporters from Rajasthan to discuss opportunities under India’s FTAs and the practical challenges involved in availing preferential market access. India’s trade agreements and arrangements with partners, including the UAE, Australia, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) countries and the United Kingdom, offer avenues for Indian goods and services to access overseas consumers, buyers, investors and value chains, subject to the provisions and implementation status of the respective agreements.
The discussions focused on identifying export-ready products, understanding tariff preferences and rules of origin, meeting quality and certification requirements, and strengthening connections with overseas buyers. These areas are important for enabling businesses to make effective use of the market access available under India’s trade agreements.
A sector-specific presentation was delivered by Joint Director General of Foreign Trade, Jaipur, Shri Md. Moin Afaque, on export opportunities for the gems and jewellery sector under India’s recently concluded FTAs. The presentation highlighted that India ranks eighth among global gems and jewellery exporters, with a 2.9% share in the US$ 1 trillion global market. It also outlined the import market opportunities available under India’s new FTAs, including immediate duty-free access across tariff lines in each of the agreements, as stated in the presentation.
The presentation examined India’s competitive position vis-à-vis major supplier countries and identified product categories and FTA markets where Indian exporters could benefit from tariff advantages. Emerging opportunities were highlighted in lab-grown diamond jewellery, coloured gemstones, Kundan-Meenakari heritage jewellery, smart and wearable jewellery, recycled and ethically sourced gold jewellery, and pearl and cultured jewellery. These opportunities are particularly relevant for Rajasthan, given the State’s established presence in the gems and jewellery sector.
Rajasthan has significant potential to contribute to India’s export growth through textiles and garments, handicrafts, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, stone and minerals, and agricultural and processed-food products. The Rajasthan Economic Review 2024–25 outlines the State’s ambition to become a US$ 350 billion economy by 2029 and achieve exports of ₹1.5 lakh crore by 2029, as envisaged under the Rajasthan Export Promotion Policy (REPP) 2024. The Rajasthan Budget 2026–27 also sets out the vision of Viksit Rajasthan @ 2047, with the goal of building a US$ 4.3 trillion economy by 2047. These objectives align with the national vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047.
FTAs can provide opportunities for Rajasthan’s farmers and farmer-producer organisations (FPOs) to access new markets for eligible agricultural produce, millets, spices and processed foods, subject to food-safety, traceability and other importing-country requirements. For MSMEs and artisans engaged in textiles, handicrafts, jewellery and engineering, tariff preferences can improve price competitiveness and support participation in international supply chains. Women-led enterprises and self-help groups can benefit from export training, e-commerce and buyer linkages, while larger businesses can explore investment, technology partnerships and market diversification. The benefits available will depend on the product, partner country and applicable FTA provisions.
By connecting enterprises in Jaipur, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Bhilwara and other districts with international buyers and supply chains, the outreach programme seeks to strengthen Rajasthan’s participation in global trade. Greater awareness of trade preferences, export documentation, product standards, logistics and market intelligence can help first-time exporters expand beyond domestic markets.
State Government support, along with initiatives for developing industrial areas and parks, sector-specific task forces focused on exports, and policies and schemes promoting credit facilities, financial incentives, market linkages, skill development, quality certification, technology upgradation and e-commerce, can further support entrepreneurship, employment and livelihoods. These efforts can contribute to Rajasthan’s development aspirations under Viksit Rajasthan 2047 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

content:
HIGHLIGHTS:
The First Stakeholder Consultation Meeting of the Climate Science into Services for India Forum (CSSIF) was held at IITM, Pune, on 17 October 2026.
The meeting focused on connecting climate science with practical services to support policy-relevant information and informed decision-making.
Technical sessions covered weather and climate products, climate models, data, and the need for a Climate Services Information System (CSIS) for the nation.
The sectoral consultation featured thematic groups addressing Health with a special focus on impact of climate extremes, Energy and Finance, Climate Projections and Service
The thematic sessions provided a platform for brainstorming and interactive discussions on sector-specific climate information needs and applications.
IITM Pune; 17.10.2026: The Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), organised the First Stakeholder Consultation Meeting of the Climate Science into Services for India Forum (CSSIF) on 17 October 2026 at its campus in Pune. This meet brought  together more than 150 participants from over 80 institutions across various states of the country which comprises of stakeholders from government ministries and departments, operational agencies, research and academic institutions, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), civil society and the private sector.
The consultation focused on the role of climate science in developing relevant climate services and strengthening the application of weather and climate information across different sectors.
The programme commenced with the welcoming and felicitation of dignitaries, followed by the welcome address by Dr. A. Suryachandra Rao, Director, IITM, Prof. V. K. Dadhwal, Former Director, Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST), Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), addressed the gathering as the Chief Guest. Dr. Suvarna Fadnavis, Project Director, Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR), IITM, presented an overview of the stakeholder consultation meeting.
The technical session featured an introductory talk by Dr. Rupa Kumar Kolli, Former Chief of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Climate Applications and Services Division, on the need for a Climate Services Information System for the nation. Shri Amardeep Raju, Scientist, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), delivered an invited talk on the need for policy-relevant climate change information. The session also covered weather and climate products at IITM-MoES and climate models, data and products, presented by Dr. Swapna Panickal, Senior Scientist at CCCR, IITM.
The sectoral consultation featured thematic breakout groups to encourage brainstorming and interactive discussions on the application of climate science to sector-specific challenges. Sectional groups on water resources and hydrology, on agriculture and food security, and on disaster management and risk reduction.With a special focus on climate extremes such as precipitation, heat and wildfires; energy and finance, including renewable energy transition, insurance and economic risk assessment; and climate projections and services, covering marine heatwaves, marine productivity, coastal vulnerability and frameworks for translating observations into services.
Through sector-wise thematic consultations, stakeholders highlighted their climate information requirements, operational challenges and expectations, while gaining greater insight into IITM’s climate research, datasets and products and their potential translation into useful and actionable climate services. The key recommendations emerging from the consultation will help strengthen the interface between climate science, services, policy and societal needs.
The meeting marks the beginning of sustained engagement under CSSIF towards developing scientifically robust, user-oriented and sector-relevant climate information and services for India.
Participants represented a wide range of major national and state-level organisations, including the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), India Meteorological Department (IMD), Naval Headquarters, National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM), Central Water and Power Research Station (CWPRS), National Water Academy, Reserve Bank of India (RBI), National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (NCPOR), Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR), National Institute of Virology (NIV), National Institute of Epidemiology (NIE), and ICAR institutes.
Strong participation was also received from state-level organisations, including State Disaster Management Authorities, state Environment, Forest and Climate Change Departments, Pune Municipal Corporation, Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre, Goa State Pollution Control Board, Madhya Pradesh Climate Change Centre, Goa State Climate Change Cell, Assam Climate Change Management Society, Bihar Mausam Seva Kendra, and other state agencies from across the country.
The consultation also included representatives from leading NGOs and civil-society organisations such as The Nature Conservancy India, Watershed Organisation Trust (WOTR), BAIF Development Research Foundation, TERRE Policy Centre, Swayam Shikshan Prayog, Development Support Centre, Naam Foundation, EarthSight Foundation, GRAAM and the Ecological Society, along with universities and research institutions including Savitribai Phule Pune University, Christian Medical College Vellore, National Institute of Advanced Studies, Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics, Krea University, and scientists from IITM.

The National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) has disbursed Rs 1.19 crore under the Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) mechanism to 29 State Biodiversity Boards and one Union Territory Biodiversity Council to support biodiversity conservation, sustainable use of biological resources and community welfare. The amount represents ABS contributions received from companies for research and commercial utilisation of agricultural biological resources.
As the biological resources were procured through markets or traders, individual benefit claimers could not be readily identified. Accordingly, the NBA adopted the distribution mechanism recommended by the Expert Committee and approved by the Authority. The allocations were determined in proportion to the estimated cultivation areas of the respective biological resources, based on official agricultural statistics published by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare through its Unified Portal for Agricultural Statistics.

The agriculture sector is emerging as a potential contributor to India’s ABS mechanism, demonstrating how the utilisation of agricultural biological resources can generate benefits for conservation and local communities. As on date, the NBA has disbursed Rs 86 crore realised from the agriculture sector to various beneficiaries. The funds allocated to the State Biodiversity Boards and the Union Territory Biodiversity Council shall be utilised exclusively for activities specified under Section 32(2) of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. These activities include biodiversity documentation, conservation and sustainable use, strengthening local biodiversity governance, research, capacity building and enhancement of community livelihoods.
The NBA has so far disbursed more than Rs 203 crore, supporting biodiversity conservation and the livelihoods of local communities. As India prepares for the seventeenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17), scheduled for 19-30 October 2026 in Yerevan, Armenia, these efforts underscore the country's commitment to conserving its biological heritage while ensuring that the benefits derived from it contribute to the well-being of local communities.

title: CAQM reviews Compliance Status and Enforcement Actions across NCR; 124 inspections conducted from 25.09.2026 to 09.10.2026
subtitle: Flying Squads directed to prioritise Red and Orange category Industries during Inspections
ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 6:03PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas (CAQM) reviewed enforcement actions, inspection findings and compliance status across the National Capital Region (NCR) at the 141st meeting of its Enforcement Task Force (ETF), held on 16.10.2026.
During the 15-day reporting period from 25.09.2026 to 09.10.2026, a total of 124 inspections were reported, comprising six inspections at Construction and Demolition (C&D) sites, 54 in the industrial sector and 64 related to Diesel Generator (DG) sets. These inspections resulted in 55 reported violations, including five at C&D sites, 35 in the industrial sector and 15 related to DG sets.
Based on the reported violations, various enforcement actions have been proposed. These include closure of two C&D projects and three industrial units; sealing of 12 units across the industrial and DG sectors; and issuance of orders or directions for compliance in one C&D case, five industrial cases and one DG-related case. Other proposed measures include imposition of Environmental Compensation (EC), re-inspection, forwarding of cases to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs), and issuance of advisories and letters to project proponents and concerned authorities.
The ETF also reviewed action taken on cases considered at its 140th meeting. The status of various enforcement measures, including closure, sealing of DG sets, issuance of EC letters and advisories, forwarding of cases to CPCB/SPCBs and re-inspection, was reviewed. The Task Force further reviewed resumption orders issued after the previous meeting. As on 15.10.2026, three resumption orders had been issued, all pertaining to C&D sites. Of these, two were in Haryana and one in Uttar Pradesh. In addition, three cases were transferred to the concerned SPCBs or authorities for a final decision. These comprised one industrial case and two C&D cases, with one case pertaining to Delhi and two to Haryana.
The ETF reviewed the updated cumulative enforcement status of the Commission’s Flying Squads. As on 16.10.2026, the Flying Squads had carried out inspections at 28,868 units, projects and entities across the NCR. Based on these inspections, 1,837 Closure Directions had been issued. Of these, 1,491 Resumption Orders had been issued following verification of compliance. A further 130 cases had been transferred to the respective SPCBs or the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) for a final decision, while 216 entities remained to be issued resumption orders.
The ETF also reviewed the status of enforcement orders issued across the concerned sectors. As on 15.10.2026, a total of 34 orders had been issued in the industrial sector, 29 in the C&D sector and 27 in respect of DG sets. The Task Force took note of the disposal and processing of these cases, including those requiring additional information, personal hearings and re-inspection.
The Commission reiterated that inspections should preferably focus on Red and Orange category industries, particularly those having furnaces and boilers. The Flying Squads were advised to strictly follow standing instructions on verifying complete and accurate addresses before submitting inspection reports, particularly in view of instances of Closure Directions and letters being returned undelivered.
The Commission emphasised the need to further strengthen enforcement, ensure timely verification of compliance and maintain close coordination among implementing agencies. It also stressed expeditious enforcement action, strict compliance monitoring and continued inspections across priority sectors, including industrial units, C&D activities and DG sets, to ensure effective mitigation of air pollution across the NCR.

Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change (EFCC), Shri Bhupender Yadav, today interacted with start-ups and innovation companies working on air pollution mitigation, with a focus on developing practical, scalable and technology-driven solutions to address the air pollution challenge in Delhi-NCR. This interaction was held under a streak of stakeholder engagement initiatives within the theme
‘Saaf Hawa mein Hissedaari, Hum Sabhi ki hai Zimmedaari’
campaign. Also present on the occasion were Union MoS (EFCC), Shri Kirti Vardhan Singh; Minister for Environment, Forest and Wildlife (GNCTD), Sardar Manjinder Singh Sirsa; besides senior officers from MoEFCC, MoHUA, MoAFW, Delhi government, CAQM, CPCB, DPCC, among others.
The interaction centred on translating innovative technologies into real-world, practically deployable and affordable solutions that can deliver measurable impact at source and in real time. Shri Yadav presented a set of
specific problem statements
covering 9 key areas of air pollution management and engaged with the innovators on how their technologies could be adapted, scaled and deployed on the ground. The Minister highlighted that the engagement sought to complement ongoing measures such as the Graded Response Action Plan, promotion of cleaner fuels and electric mobility, and strengthening of air-quality monitoring with source-level technological interventions.
The
proposed solutions
spanned the entire air-pollution management chain - from detection and monitoring to prediction, enforcement and mitigation. They included tamper-proof systems for Online Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (OCEMS), Air Pollution Control Devices (APCD) and Pollution Under Control (PUC) testing; AI-enabled identification of industrial emission violations; real-time monitoring of combustion efficiency and diesel generator emission-control devices; and technologies for detecting and controlling dust at construction and demolition sites. Innovative approaches for low-cost mechanised road sweeping, monitoring road-dust resuspension, portable pothole repair and modular dust-containment systems were also discussed.
Addressing the meeting, Shri Bhupender Yadav highlighted that the interaction with start-ups is a novel, proactive initiative aimed at bridging the gap between policymakers and technology innovators. He said that such engagement can help bring greater uniformity in policy implementation and enhance transparency in governance. Stressing the need for stronger technology-enabled enforcement, he said that integration of OCEMS data with plant-operation data is essential to identify malpractices, and AI can play an important role in achieving this objective.
The Union Minister emphasised the importance of city-wide air-quality monitoring and called for cleaner vehicles and smoother traffic management, including tamper-proof PUC monitoring and AI-based prediction of traffic congestion hotspots. He said that start-ups need to focus on environment-friendly solutions for scientific management of crop-residue, solid-waste and construction & demolition waste. He also stressed the need for guidelines on parali storage involving MoAFW, CAQM and CPCB, along with development of an in-situ crop-residue storage model. Shri Yadav further highlighted the need for faster and more efficient road maintenance as an important measure for active road-dust control.
Briefing the media, Shri Yadav informed that the
major focus of the interaction
was on using artificial intelligence, sensors, remote sensing, satellite and drone-based technologies and data analytics to move towards real-time understanding of air pollution. He stated that solutions presented by the innovators include hyperlocal air-quality monitoring, city-wide pollution mapping, hotspot identification and forecasting, AI-based source apportionment, real-time identification of pollution sources and predictive traffic-congestion management. Technologies were displayed for 24x7 detection of stubble and open biomass burning, as well as automated identification of vehicles without valid PUC certificates and over-aged vehicles, which could further strengthen timely enforcement and intervention, he added.
The Minister also talked about the solutions that sought to address the waste and residue dimensions of air pollution. These included
technology-enabled systems
to connect recycled construction and demolition waste products with construction-sector demand, municipal solid waste management, and integrated systems for collection, transportation and productive utilisation of paddy straw for bioenergy, biomass fuel, composting and other value-added applications like environmental-friendly packaging, thereby reducing the need for open-field burning. Start-ups working on crop-residue-based materials and biochar-based solutions also brought about opportunities to convert agricultural residue into productive uses rather than treating it as waste.
Shri Yadav further informed that the participating innovators
showcased capabilities
ranging from AI and machine learning, IoT-based environmental monitoring and pollution analytics to drone-based aerial mapping, remote sensing, advanced sensing systems and source-level pollution-control technologies. The Minister noted that the interaction underscored the need to move beyond isolated technological solutions towards
integrated, scalable and economically viable interventions
that can be deployed across Delhi-NCR. He encouraged the innovators to align their technologies with clearly identified field-level requirements and explore how successful solutions can be taken to scale through appropriate implementation and monitoring mechanisms.
The engagement marks an effort to bring together government, technology innovators and field-level implementation in a
Jan Bhagidari
mode to develop actionable solutions for Delhi-NCR’s air pollution challenge.

title: Clarification on Legislative Developments concerning Government’s shareholding in IDBI
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 7:41AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Certain sections of press and media have brought out reports, which inter alia have comments/ views regarding the legislative developments in 2003 concerning the Government’s shareholding in IDBI. It is reiterted that during the disucssions of Union Budget, 2003 and the parliamentary debate on the IDBI (Repeal) Act, 2003, an amendment seeking to restrict the dilution of the Government’s stake was moved but was ultimately rejected and did not form part of the enacted legislation.
The matter was subsequently examined by the Delhi High Court in All India IDBI Officers’ Association v. Union of India & Others, decided on 17 December 2018. The Court, while dismissing the writ petition, adjudicated in paragraphs 41 and 42 as follows:
Paragraph 41:
“This Court is of the view that the statements made before the House almost 15 years earlier, in a debate relating to a legislative activity, would not preclude the Central Government from diluting its stake in IDBI Ltd. Indisputably, the legislation enacted by the Parliament after the debate did not contain the amendment that was sought to be introduced. The statements made before the House cannot substitute or override the statue so enacted by the Parliament. Surely, the Parliament was conscious of the import of not including the proviso as proposed. The principles of promissory estoppel are wholly inapplicable in the aforesaid context. It is not possible to accept that the statements made in Parliament amounted to a representation made to the employees and they had acted to their prejudice based on such representation. The statements made before the House were in the context of enacting a legislation (the IDBI Repeal Act, 2003), and the said Act has to be interpreted in conformity with the settled principles of statutory interpretation.”
Paragraph 42:
“There is no ambiguity in the language of the IDBI Repeal Act, 2003 and there is no scope to read any provision into the said enactment which proscribes the Government from reducing or divesting its stake in IDBI Ltd.”
The aforesaid judgment is significant as it specifically addresses the doctrine of promissory estoppel, which was relied upon in challenging the Government’s decision to dilute its shareholding. The doctrine could not be invoked to prevent the Government from reducing or divesting its stake in IDBI Ltd.
The Government’s policy towards the transformation and strategic disinvestment of IDBI Bank was reiterated in successive Union Budget Speeches in the Parliament:
Union Budget 2016–17 — Speech of the then Hon’ble Finance Minister, Shri Arun Jaitley (Paragraph 93) said:
“Our Public Sector Banks will have to be strong and competitive. The Bank Board Bureau will be operationalized during 2016-17 and a roadmap for consolidation of Public Sector Banks will be spelt out. The process of transformation of IDBI Bank has already started. Government will take it forward and also consider the option of reducing its stake to below 50%.”
Union Budget 2021–22 — Speech of the then Hon’ble Finance Minister, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman (Paragraph 84) said:
“In spite of COVID-19, we have kept working towards strategic disinvestment. A number of transactions namely BPCL, Air India, Shipping Corporation of India, Container Corporation of India, IDBI Bank, BEML, Pawan Hans, Neelachal Ispat Nigam limited among others would be completed in 2021-22. Other than IDBI Bank, we propose to take up the privatization of two Public Sector Banks and one General Insurance company in the year 2021-22. This would require legislative amendments and I propose to introduce the amendments in this Session itself.”
The legislative history of the IDBI (Repeal) Act, 2003, the judicial pronouncement of the Hon’ble Delhi High Court and successive Union Budget Speeches collectively demonstrate the evolution of the Government’s policy towards the strategic disinvestment of IDBI Bank. The Judgment dated 17 December 2018 clarifies beyond doubt that the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked on the basis of statements made during parliamentary debates to restrict the Government’s power to dilute its shareholding in the IDBI Bank Ltd.The Court further held that the enacted legislation contained no prohibition against reducing the Government’s stake in the IDBI Bank Ltd.

title: FSSAI Proposes Science-Based Pesticide Residue Limits for Tea, Reaffirming Commitment to Consumer Safety
subtitle:
FSSAI Notifies Draft Amendment Proposing Maximum Residue Limits for Acetamiprid and Imidacloprid in Tea; Invites Stakeholder Comments

India Proposes Acetamiprid Residue Limit of 20 ppm in Tea, Lower than Corresponding Limits of 30 ppm in Japan and 50 ppm in the USA

Earlier Regulatory Measures Included Delisting of 13 Pesticides with Higher Toxicity, Reflecting Continued Focus on Food Safety

India's Average Pesticide Use of Less Than 0.5 kg per Hectare Substantially Below Global Average of 2.38 kg per Hectare

Proposed Standards Seek to Balance Consumer Safety with Effective Pest Management and Sustainable Agricultural Practices
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 3:26PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), as part of its ongoing efforts to promote science-based food safety regulation and consumer protection, has notified draft amendments proposing Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) for two pesticides, Acetamiprid and Imidacloprid, in tea. The proposal reflects FSSAI's approach towards reviewing pesticide residue standards in light of scientific assessments, relevant international practices and the requirements of Indian agriculture.
The draft Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette of India on 16 October 2026, propose MRLs of 20 mg/kg (20 ppm) for Acetamiprid and 50 mg/kg (50 ppm) for Imidacloprid in tea. The proposed limits are intended to provide clearly defined regulatory benchmarks for pesticide residues, facilitating compliance, monitoring and enforcement of food safety requirements, subject to finalisation of the draft regulations.
Notably, the proposed MRL of 20 ppm for Acetamiprid in tea is lower than the corresponding limits of 30 ppm in Japan and 50 ppm in the United States of America. The proposed limit for Imidacloprid has also been formulated with reference to international Codex standards. These comparisons reflect the emphasis on considering internationally recognised regulatory practices while taking into account India's food safety priorities and domestic agricultural requirements.
The latest proposal forms part of FSSAI's broader regulatory approach towards the review and revision of pesticide residue standards. The Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Amendment Regulations, 2024, represented an important step in this process, involving a review of MRLs in light of available scientific data and international practices. Earlier regulatory measures also included the delisting of 13 pesticides identified as having higher toxicity, reflecting the continuing emphasis on appropriate regulatory safeguards and consumer protection.
Maximum Residue Limits are an important component of food safety regulation. They specify the maximum legally permitted concentration of pesticide residues in food commodities and are established on the basis of scientific assessments, taking into account pesticide residue data, dietary exposure and relevant safety considerations. These standards provide a measurable regulatory basis for monitoring pesticide residues and ensuring compliance with prescribed food safety requirements.
The proposed standards also recognise the importance of effective pest management in agricultural production. Pesticides, when used appropriately and in accordance with prescribed practices, help farmers protect crops against pests, minimise crop losses and maintain agricultural productivity. Access to suitable crop-protection measures can also support cost-effective farming practices. The regulatory approach therefore seeks to balance the requirements of agricultural production with the overarching priority of consumer safety.
India's comparatively low average pesticide use provides an important perspective on the country's agricultural practices. At less than 0.5 kg per hectare, India's average pesticide use is significantly below the estimated global average of 2.38 kg per hectare. It is also lower than the levels reported in several countries, including Colombia, Brazil and the United States of America.
Internationally, countries such as the United States, Japan and China, as well as members of the European Union, have registered a wide range of pesticides suited to their respective crops, climatic conditions and agricultural requirements. India's regulatory approach similarly seeks to take into account domestic crop-protection needs while maintaining appropriate safeguards for consumers through scientifically established residue limits.
For the tea sector, the proposed limits are intended to provide greater regulatory clarity to growers, processors, food businesses, testing laboratories and enforcement authorities. Clearly defined standards can facilitate consistent monitoring, responsible pesticide management and adherence to food safety requirements, while supporting confidence in the quality and safety of Indian tea.
The draft amendment reflects FSSAI's continued focus on evidence-based regulation, consumer protection and responsible agricultural practices. By combining scientific assessment, international regulatory considerations and stakeholder consultation, the proposed framework seeks to balance food safety priorities with the practical requirements of tea cultivation, while contributing to India's broader objective of maintaining a transparent and responsive food safety regulatory ecosystem.

title: FSSAI Moves to Strengthen Infant Nutrition Standards by Restricting Addition of Sucrose and Fructose in Products for Infants Up to Six Months
subtitle:
FSSAI Notifies Draft Amendment to Infant Nutrition Regulations, Proposing Stronger Safeguards Against Added Sugars During Early Infancy

Proposed Restriction Aims to Promote Appropriate Infant Nutrition and Support Healthy Growth and Development During the Crucial First Six Months of Life

Initiative Reinforces Government's Commitment to Preventive Healthcare, Child Nutrition and Long-Term Health and Well-being
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 1:59PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In a significant step towards strengthening nutritional safeguards for infants, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has published a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, proposing to prohibit the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age.
The draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette of India on 16 October 2026, seek to further strengthen the existing regulatory framework by ensuring that infant nutrition products are formulated in accordance with age-appropriate nutritional requirements, with particular emphasis on minimising exposure to added sugars during the earliest stages of life.
The existing regulations prescribe comprehensive nutritional composition, quality and safety standards for various categories of infant nutrition products intended for children from birth up to 24 months of age. Under the current provisions, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred sources of carbohydrates, while sucrose and/or fructose may be added only when required as a carbohydrate source, subject to prescribed limits.
Building upon these provisions, the draft amendment proposes a specific restriction on the addition of sucrose and fructose in products intended for infants up to six months of age. The proposed provision states that "sucrose and fructose shall not be added in the products intended for infants up to the age of 6 months".
The first six months of life represent a critical period for healthy growth and development, making appropriate nutrition particularly important. The proposed restriction seeks to ensure that infant nutrition products meet the nutritional needs of this age group without unnecessary addition of sucrose and fructose. The measure is also intended to support broader public health efforts to address concerns associated with early exposure to added sugars, including dietary risk factors linked to childhood obesity and related health challenges.
The initiative complements established public health recommendations promoting exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life. By strengthening standards for infant nutrition products, the proposed amendment seeks to support appropriate infant feeding practices while encouraging manufacturers to adopt formulations that prioritise the specific nutritional requirements of young infants.
The proposed regulatory measure reflects FSSAI's continued focus on science-based food standards, responsible product formulation and preventive nutrition. It also underlines the importance of safeguarding the nutritional well-being of children from the earliest stages of life as an integral component of the country's broader public health priorities.
The draft notification has been published for public consultation, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders within 60 days from the date on which copies of the Official Gazette containing the notification are made available to the public. The representations received within the prescribed period will be considered by FSSAI before finalisation of the amendment.

He said the Mela provides a marketing platform for artisans and beneficiaries from Scheduled Castes (SCs), Other Backward Classes (OBCs) and Safai Karamcharis, enabling them to showcase their traditional handicrafts, handloom products and other goods to a wider audience.
The Official said the Mela has been jointly organized by three national corporations under the Ministry namely National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation (NSFDC), the National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC) and the National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC), which provide financial assistance to artisans and eligible beneficiaries.

The Ministry has been organizing Shilp Samagam Melas since 2022, benefiting 975 artisans through 13 fairs held so far.

content:
The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, through MY Bharat and the National Service Scheme (NSS), launched Month 2 of the Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat 100 Week Sankalp Abhiyan with the nationwide observance of “Yoga evam Aatm-Suraksha Diwas” (Yoga and Self-Defence Day) on October 16, 2026. Inaugurated by the Hon’ble Prime Minister, the campaign has entered its second month under the theme “Fit Youth, Addiction-Free Youth (Shakti evam Seva),” focusing on physical fitness, mental resilience, discipline and self-confidence as key elements of a healthy, addiction-free society.
The Week 5 intervention witnessed the participation of 91,179 people across 183 educational institutions, NSS units and adopted villages nationwide. The activities brought together local leaders, police officials, sports authorities, medical experts and certified yoga instructors to promote healthy lifestyles, personal safety and awareness about substance abuse.
As part of the initiative, 332 yoga sessions engaged 34,290 participants, including 19,882 women, while 311 self-defence demonstrations reached 31,507 participants, including 18,364 women. An additional 180 community awareness activities engaged 25,391 participants. The yoga sessions incorporated the Common Yoga Protocol and relaxation techniques to highlight the importance of physical well-being and stress management. Self-defence demonstrations focused on practical safety techniques, situational awareness and personal security, particularly for young women.
Women accounted for 57.1% of the total participation, reflecting their strong engagement in the campaign. Regional Directorates, including Delhi, Jaipur, Lucknow, Patna and Trivandrum, recorded notable female participation. The activities were supported by partner organisations, including Anuvrat Vishva Bharati Society, BAPS, Bharat Scouts & Guides and MY Bharat Kendras.
The nationwide observance also generated significant digital outreach, with 4,197 social media posts shared organically under the campaign hashtag #NashaMuktYuva.
By integrating yoga, self-defence and community awareness, the initiative reinforces the role of physical fitness, mental well-being and personal resilience in preventing substance abuse. Through the 100 Week Sankalp Abhiyan, MY Bharat and NSS continue to mobilise young people and communities towards the vision of a Viksit Bharat and an addiction-free India, guided by the NSS motto, “Not Me, But You.”.

title: Connecting Kashmir: Building the Infrastructure for Growth
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                17 OCT 2026 11:21AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Jammu and Kashmir's challenging terrain is steadily yielding to a new era of connectivity. The Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link has connected the valley to India's rail network. Its centrepiece, the Chenab Bridge, stands as the world's highest railway arch bridge. Expanded Vande Bharat services are improving passenger mobility. New freight terminals are carrying Kashmiri apples, saffron and handicrafts to national markets, opening opportunities for farmers and businesses. On land, the Sonamarg and Zojila tunnels promise year-round passage into Ladakh. In the air, Srinagar's expanding airport is complemented by nascent hubs at Udhampur and Kishtwar. Together, these advances are drawing Kashmir's produce, trade and tourism firmly into the national mainstream.
A Region Reconnected
Jammu and Kashmir's mountainous terrain has long made connectivity a major infrastructure challenge. Over the years, this has been steadily changing, with a wave of infrastructure investment reshaping how the region connects with the rest of the country. The Udhampur–Srinagar–Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) project is a major part of this expansion. It is one of the most challenging railway line projects undertaken in the country post-independence. Today it stands as one of India’s engineering marvels, linking the Kashmir Valley to the rest of the country by rail.
The USBRL project has also been accompanied by sustained expansion of roads, tunnels and airport infrastructure. The network now includes new train services such as the Vande Bharat Express. It also includes major road corridors and tunnels. Airport capacity is being expanded at Srinagar, with regional airports planned under UDAN, increasing passenger movement. Multimodal cargo terminals and enhanced freight services support goods movement across the region. These developments have progressively expanded all-weather connectivity infrastructure across Jammu and Kashmir.
Railways: Connecting Kashmir to the National Rail Network
Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) National Project
The USBRL project was inaugurated in
June 2025
, improving connectivity infrastructure in the Himalayan region. Built at a cost of
₹43,780
crore
, the USBRL project covers the districts of
Udhampur
,
Reasi
,
Ramban
,
Srinagar
,
Anantnag
,
Pulwama
,
Budgam
and
Baramulla
of Jammu and Kashmir.
The project stretches
272 kilometres
through the rugged Himalayas; it includes
36 tunnels
that span 119 kilometres and
943 bridges
. Designed to overcome the region’s challenging terrain, it connects remote areas with the national rail network. It is opening new opportunities for mobility, trade and tourism. As part of the USBRL project, over
215 km (including a tunnel and 320 bridges) of roads
have been constructed, which are useful for communities. Additionally, the
USBRL project
is fully electrified both in tunnels and in open stretches.
The USBRL project has made substantial socio-economic contributions to the region, with employment generation being a significant aspect of its impact. The project has generated more than 5 crore man-days of employment.
Vande Bharat Express
Image 1:
Vande Bharat Express, Jammu and Kashmir
The Vande Bharat Express in Jammu and Kashmir first began operations in June 2025, between Katra and Srinagar. To further enhance railway connectivity, the Srinagar-Katra Vande Bharat Express service was extended to Jammu Tawi Railway Station in April 2026.
The distance from Jammu to Srinagar is now covered in less than
five hours
. The trains have been augmented from 8 to 20 coaches. They are specially designed to operate in extreme weather conditions. The trains are equipped with advanced operating systems and electronics suited for high-altitude conditions.
Supporting this route is a snow removal train that moves ahead to clear the tracks, ensuring year-round services. Seismic dampers have also been installed to absorb tremors, offering a safer and smoother journey in this high-risk zone.
Engineering Marvels under the USBRL Project
The USBRL project includes several major engineering achievements, including the Chenab Rail Bridge, Anji Khad Bridge and Tunnel T50.
Chenab Rail Bridge
Under the USBRL project, the
world’s highest railway arch bridge
has been built over the Chenab River in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir. The Chenab bridge, inaugurated in
June 2025,
is
1,315 m long.
It has an arch span of 467 metres and rises 359 metres above the riverbed, making it higher than the Eiffel Tower. The bridge is designed to withstand strong seismic and wind forces. With Vande Bharat services running over the bridge, connectivity has significantly improved between Jammu and Kashmir.
Image 2:
Chenab Rail Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir
Anji Khad Bridge
Image 3:
Anji Khad Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir
The Anji Khad bridge is India’s
first cable-stayed railway bridge
built above the Anji River gorge, a tributary of the Chenab River. The Anji Khad bridge is part of the USBRL project and was inaugurated in
June 2025.
The bridge is located in the
Reasi
district
of Jammu and Kashmir. It is supported by a single 193-metre-high tower shaped like an
inverted ‘Y’,
with cables supporting the bridge. The main bridge has a
total length of 473.25 metres,
designed for the region’s challenging terrain and seismic conditions.
Tunnel T50
Image 4:
Tunnel T50 in Jammu and Kashmir
Tunnel T50, inaugurated in 2024, is a
12.77-km rail
tunnel linking
Khari
and
Sumber
in Jammu and Kashmir. It is India’s
longest transportation tunnel
, built under the USBRL project. The tunnel provides a vital rail link between the Kashmir Valley and the rest of India.
The New Austrian Tunnelling Method has been used to construct the tunnel through the challenging Himalayan geology. The tunnel engineering overcame the challenges of high-water ingress, landslides, shear zones, and jointed volcanic rocks. The tunnel features a main tube paired with a parallel escape tunnel, linked every 375 metres for safety. CCTV cameras are placed every 50 metres, which help monitor from a central control room.
Supporting Railway Infrastructure
Railway connectivity in Jammu and Kashmir is being strengthened through increased investment in supporting infrastructure and network development. The annual average budget of railways for Jammu and Kashmir has increased from ₹1,044 crore in 2009–14 to ₹1,086 crore in 2026–27.
Electrification
Indian Railways has pursued railway electrification in mission mode, with about 99.6% of the Broad Gauge (BG) network now electrified.
In Jammu and Kashmir, the entire existing BG network is electrified
. All new-line and multi-tracking projects are being sanctioned and built with electrification from the outset.
Station Redevelopment
Under the
Amrit Bharat Station Scheme
,
1,340 stations
have been identified for redevelopment across Indian Railways. Among them,
four stations
are in
Jammu and Kashmir
. The stations are
Budgam
,
Jammu
Tawi
,
Martyr Captain Tushar Mahajan (Udhampur)
and
Shri Mata Vaishno
Devi Katra
station.
Other Regional
Railway Initiatives
To strengthen railway connectivity in border areas and areas of strategic significance in Jammu and Kashmir, several projects are in the pipeline. These include
A
third line between Jalandhar Cantt. and Jammu Tawi (216 km).
An
additional line between Jammu and Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra (78 km).
A
new railway line between Jammu/Reasi and Poonch (190 km)
.
Roads: Strengthening Surface Connectivity
Roads as a complement to Rail
In Jammu and Kashmir, road infrastructure is expanding alongside railway infrastructure. Roads remain essential for last-mile access to places outside the railway network. In
August 2026
, foundation stones were laid for
110 road projects covering 598.455 km
under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY)-IV. Costing more than
₹1,500 crore
, the projects are expected to benefit
46,972 people
across the Udhampur–Kathua–Doda–Kishtwar region. The projects also include the
use of waste plastics
in several road packages, supporting more sustainable road construction.
Tunnel construction has also become a key component of development in the Himalayan region to ensure all-weather connectivity, improve road safety, and enhance strategic mobility.
Sonamarg (Z-Morh) Tunnel
Image 5:
Sonamarg Tunnel, Jammu and Kashmir
The Sonamarg tunnel project, also known as the Z-Morh, inaugurated in January 2025, is a
6.4 km bi-directional tunnel with a parallel escape tunnel of length 6.4 km and an approach road of length 5.5km
. Constructed at a cost of over
₹2,700 crore
, the tunnel sits at an altitude of 2634 meters above sea level. The tunnel provides
all-weather connectivity
between Srinagar and Sonamarg enroute to Leh. It bypasses parts of the road hit by major avalanches and landslides. It promotes tourism by transforming Sonamarg into a year-round destination, boosting winter tourism, adventure sports and local livelihoods. Along with the Zojila Tunnel,
it will cut the NH-1 section of this project from 13 km to 11.98 km
.
Zojila Tunnel
The Zojila Tunnel is a 13.153-kilometre-long bi-directional tunnel being constructed between Baltal and Minamarg on National Highway-1 by NHIDCL. Elevated at 2,900–3,310 metres, the ₹6,808-crore project will provide all-weather year-round road connectivity between Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. With construction beginning in October 2020, the main tunnel achieved breakthrough in June 2026.
Image 6:
Zojila Tunnel, Jammu and Kashmir
The tunnel will be equipped with modern ventilation systems, automatic fire detection and suppression systems, CCTV surveillance, a Variable Message Sign (VMS) system, SCADA system, and other advanced safety and traffic management systems. The project also includes
two twin tube uni-directional Nilgari tunnels of total length 4.8 km,  eight cut-and-cover sections with a total length of 2.350 km, four bridges with a total length of 810 m, 40 culverts, snow galleries, catch dams, deflector dams, air-blast walls, and other avalanche protection structures along the approach road of length 16.964 km.
Upon completion, the project is expected to reduce the travel time between
Sonamarg and Minamarg from approximately two hours to around 30 minutes
. The project will also reduce the risks of accidents and disruptions associated with the treacherous Zojila Pass, which remains vulnerable to
heavy snowfall and avalanches
during the winter months. The tunnel will boost tourism, trade, and access to remote and border areas. Year-round connectivity will strengthen defence logistics and strategic preparedness. It will also create employment opportunities, support economic growth, and improve livelihoods and quality of life for local communities.
Dr Syama Prasad Mookerjee Tunnel (earlier known as Chenani-Nashri Tunnel)
The 9 km tunnel, opened in
2017
, is
India's longest operating highway tunnel
and
Asia's longest bi-directional tunnel
. It connects Udhampur to Ramban in Jammu and Kashmir.  Built at a cost of ₹2500 crore, it reduces travel distance by 31 km and cuts the travel time by two hours, saving fuel costs.
Expanding the Highway Network
Delhi–Amritsar–Katra Expressway:
The expressway is a 667-km greenfield highway connecting Delhi with Amritsar and Katra. It is designed to provide a faster road link, reduce congestion on NH-44, and improve access to major destinations, including the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi shrine. In
July 2026, key sections of the expressway were inaugurated
, marking a major step towards improving connectivity between Delhi and Katra. The completed sections are expected to
reduce travel time between Delhi and Katra from about 14 hours to nearly six hours
. The corridor will also
strengthen connectivity for pilgrims and facilitate industrial and logistics activity along the route
.
Rafiabad–Kupwara Road (NH-701):
The foundation stone for the widening and strengthening of the Rafiabad–Kupwara section of NH-701 was laid in
June 2025
to strengthen last-mile connectivity, particularly in border areas. The project forms part of the
Rafiabad–Kupwara–Chowkibal–Tangdhar–Chamkot corridor
under Project Beacon.
Shopian Bypass (NH-444):
Sanctioned in March 2024 at a cost of ₹224.44 crore, the 8.925-km Shopian bypass had its foundation stone laid in June 2025. The bypass will improve connectivity between Shopian, Pulwama and Kulgam and facilitate faster transportation of agricultural produce.
Airports: Expanding Air Connectivity
Expansion of Srinagar International Airport
A ₹1,677 crore expansion of the Civil Enclave at Srinagar International Airport was approved in February 2026. The project is operated by the Airports Authority of India within Budgam Airbase of the Indian Air Force (IAF). It will strengthen aviation connectivity in the Kashmir Valley.
Spread over 73.18 acres, the development includes a new 71,500 square metre terminal building. The terminal will handle up to 2,900 passengers during peak hours and 10 million passengers annually. The airport will also have 15 aircraft parking bays, including space for one widebody aircraft. Its existing 3,658-metre runway will continue to be operated by the Indian Air Force. A new multi-level parking facility will also provide space for 1,000 cars. The project also includes barracks for security personnel.
The new terminal will combine modern airport facilities with elements of Kashmir’s traditional architecture, including local woodwork and craftsmanship. Sustainability is a core part of the project. It includes water harvesting, greater use of natural light, and locally sourced eco-friendly materials. The project is targeted to achieve a 5-star Green Rating for Integrated Habitat Assessment (GRIHA) for sustainable building practices.
Extending Regional Air Connectivity
The Government is focusing on improving regional connectivity and providing affordable and secure travel options to residents of Jammu and Kashmir.
Udhampur and Kishtwar reflect how regional aviation can extend access to areas beyond the region’s major urban centres. The two airports are planned under the UDAN scheme to extend regional air connectivity in Jammu and Kashmir. Greater airport capacity is expected to support tourism, create employment, encourage investment and strengthen Srinagar’s role as an economic destination.
From Connectivity to Economic Integration
Multimodal Logistics
PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan, launched in October 2021, brought railways, roads, ports, waterways, airports and logistics infrastructure onto a single, Geographic Information System (GIS) based planning platform. It spans 44 Central Ministries and 36 States and UTs. Building on this framework, the Gati Shakti Multi-Modal Cargo Terminal (GCT) policy, launched in December 2021, encourages the development of modern, rail-linked cargo terminals through private investment.
So far, 142 Gati Shakti Cargo Terminals have been commissioned in the country. In 2024, a Gati Shakti Multi-Modal Cargo Terminal (GCT) was commissioned in Samba in Jammu and Kashmir and is now fully operational. In addition, In-Principle Approvals have been granted for the development of GCTs at 310 more locations, including three at Kathua, Anantnag and Jammu districts in Jammu and Kashmir.
The GCT policy has benefited key sectors such as cement, steel, power, mining, agriculture, logistics and manufacturing. It has enabled modern multimodal cargo terminals with warehousing, silos, cold storage and other value-added logistics facilities. This has increased the competitiveness of local industries and farmers while generating employment and promoting regional economic development.
From Access to Opportunities
A region once defined by seasonal isolation is emerging as a connected part of India's economic geography. Rail, road and air projects are no longer separate initiatives; together, they now function as one integrated network. This convergence is reshaping daily life for residents, farmers, traders and tourism operators alike. The expansion is increasing the access of farmers and local businesses to markets beyond the region. Signature Kashmir products, including apples, dry fruits, pashmina shawls and handicrafts, are being sold at larger markets, promoting economic diversity. At the same time, improved connectivity is strengthening the region's strategic position, including border security and disaster response.
